**Tokenization chooses the pieces the language model sees.** BPE starts with small symbols and repeatedly merges frequent adjacent pairs. A common word may become one piece while an unfamiliar word remains several. WordPiece also builds subword vocabularies using a different training criterion and commonly applies longest-match segmentation. Unigram starts with candidate pieces and prunes them under a probabilistic model of segmentation. SentencePiece is a toolkit, not a fourth single algorithm. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.06226)

Imagine a language whose common words are poorly represented in the vocabulary. A short sentence may require many pieces, using more context and decoding steps than an equivalent sentence in a well-covered language. A larger vocabulary can include useful multilingual and code substrings, shortening those sequences. But allocating the extra entries poorly may bring little improvement for the language you care about.

**Compression has a cost.** With hidden width d and vocabulary size V, an embedding table has Vd entries; an untied output table adds another such matrix. Rare vocabulary entries may receive little training. Compare token counts by language, model memory, output-computation cost, and actual quality together.

Byte-level approaches can represent arbitrary text without a fixed subword inventory but initially face longer sequences. Architectures that group bytes into latent patches aim to reduce that computational burden. Vocabulary-free input does not mean computation-free processing, and more vocabulary entries do not universally imply better models.

**Technical details and references.**

BPE repeatedly merges frequent symbol pairs. WordPiece selects subwords using a likelihood-related training criterion and commonly decodes via longest matching pieces. Unigram tokenization starts from a candidate vocabulary and prunes it under a probabilistic segmentation model; SentencePiece is a toolkit supporting multiple algorithms, not one algorithm itself. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.06226)

Byte-level/token-free models avoid a fixed subword vocabulary but face longer raw sequences; latent patching can group bytes adaptively. A larger vocabulary can encode frequent multilingual/code substrings more compactly, at the cost of larger embedding/output matrices and fewer observations per rare token.

Compression depends on training corpus and vocabulary allocation, not size alone. Evaluate bytes or characters per token by language, normalization reversibility, rare scripts, latency, and downstream accuracy.
